title: The duty of candour
blurb: Tell apart the professional and statutory duties of candour and know exactly how to be open when care goes wrong.
question: A nurse realises she gave a patient a dose of medicine an hour after it had already been given by a colleague. The patient needs extra monitoring overnight. After making him safe, what does the professional duty of candour require?

teach.body: Candour means being open and honest when something goes wrong with care that causes, or could cause, harm or distress. There are two duties. The professional duty applies to every individual nurse, midwife and nursing associate (Code 14) and is overseen by the NMC. The statutory duty in England applies to the registered provider organisation, under regulation 20 of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014, and is enforced by the CQC.
teach.cite: NMC Code 14; NMC/GMC candour guidance (updated December 2024); reg 20

rows.label: Trigger
values: Harm or potential harm or distress

rows.label: Includes near misses?
values: Report them; tell patient by judgement

items: 14.1 Act immediately to put right the situation if someone has suffered harm or an incident had the potential for harm.
14.2 Explain fully and promptly what has happened, including the likely effects, and apologise to the person (and, where appropriate, their advocate, family or carers).
14.3 Document the events formally and escalate if appropriate so they can be dealt with quickly.

teach.body: Speak to the person as soon as possible; you do not have to wait for an investigation, but be clear about what is and is not yet known. Patients expect three things: what happened, what can be done about any harm, and what will be done to stop it happening to someone else. A personal 'I am sorry' means more than an organisational expression of regret. Apologising is not an admission of legal liability, and a fitness to practise panel may see it as evidence of insight.

teach.caption: In a team, the most appropriate person (usually the lead clinician) speaks to the patient, but every registrant must make sure someone has taken this on.

teach.h: Regulation 20: notifiable safety incident (health service body)
head: Harm level
Meaning
rows: Permanent lessening of bodily, sensory, motor or intellectual function
Moderate increase in treatment, significant but not permanent harm
teach.caption: Moderate increase in treatment includes unplanned return to surgery or readmission, a longer stay, cancelled treatment or transfer such as to ICU.

teach.h: What the provider must do under reg 20

items.label: Notify the relevant person in person
True account of facts, further enquiries, an apology
Written notification with results and an apology
Keep secure records and copies of letters

teach.h: Worked scenario: Staff Nurse Femi on a surgical ward
teach.body: Femi gives Mr Doyle, 70, a second dose of an opioid an hour after a colleague's dose. He checks Mr Doyle's breathing and sedation, informs the nurse in charge and the doctor, and starts the agreed monitoring. That evening Femi tells Mr Doyle what happened, says 'I am sorry', explains the extra checks and what the ward will do to prevent it recurring, and documents the conversation and completes an incident report.

teach.text: An apology is NOT an admission of legal liability. And the professional duty is not limited to the reg 20 harm thresholds: it covers harm or distress, and near misses must still be reported.

items: Professional duty: every registrant, Code 14, NMC/GMC guidance. Statutory duty: the organisation, reg 20, CQC.
Put it right, tell the person promptly, apologise, explain the likely effects, record and escalate.
Reg 20: in-person notification with an apology, then written notification; moderate harm and 28-day psychological harm thresholds.
Never discourage a colleague from reporting; an attempted cover-up is treated seriously by the NMC.

summary: You can now distinguish the professional duty of candour held by every registrant from the statutory duty held by providers under regulation 20. You can also describe how to apologise, what to record and how the notifiable safety incident thresholds work.

A.q: Who holds the statutory duty of candour under regulation 20 in England?
options: Each registered nurse on the ward
The registered provider organisation
The Nursing and Midwifery Council
The Care Quality Commission
A.why: Regulation 20 places the statutory duty on registered persons (the provider organisations), and the CQC enforces it. Individual registrants hold the professional duty.

whyNot.0: Individual nurses hold the professional duty under Code 14, not the statutory one.
whyNot.2: The NMC oversees the professional duty; it is not the duty holder.
whyNot.3: The CQC regulates and enforces the statutory duty; it does not hold it.

options: A written admission of fault
A statement of legal liability
An offer of compensation
An expression of sorrow or regret
A.why: Regulation 20(7) defines an apology as an expression of sorrow or regret in respect of a notifiable safety incident.

whyNot.0: An apology is not an admission of fault under the regulation.
whyNot.1: Apologising does not mean admitting legal liability.
whyNot.2: Compensation is a separate matter from the apology required.

A.q: A nurse realises she gave the wrong dose of a medicine. What should she do first?
options: Act to make the patient safe
Complete an incident report
Apologise to the patient's family
Inform the ward pharmacist
A.why: Code 14.1: act immediately to put right the situation if someone has suffered actual harm or there was potential for harm. Explaining, apologising and recording follow.

whyNot.1: Reporting is required, but making the patient safe comes first.
whyNot.2: Apologising matters, but the immediate priority is the patient's safety.
whyNot.3: The pharmacist may be informed later; clinical safety comes first.

B.q: A patient asks the nurse who made the error whether saying sorry means the hospital is admitting it was negligent. What is the most accurate reply?
options: Yes, an apology accepts legal responsibility
Yes, unless the apology is given in writing
No, apologising is not an admission of liability
No, as nurses are not allowed to apologise
B.why: NMC/GMC candour guidance states that apologising does not mean admitting legal liability; NHS Resolution also advises that saying sorry is the right thing to do.

whyNot.0: An apology is not an acceptance of legal liability.
whyNot.1: Whether written or spoken, an apology is not an admission of liability.
whyNot.3: Nurses are expected to apologise under Code 14.2.

B.q: After a fall caused by a missed bed-rail check, the investigation will take weeks. When should the nurse speak to the patient?
options: As soon as possible, saying what is known so far
Once the investigation report has been completed
When the patient's family next visit the ward
When the risk management team gives permission
B.why: Speak to the patient as soon as possible. You do not have to wait for the outcome of an investigation, but be clear about what has and has not been established.

whyNot.1: Waiting for the investigation delays openness and is not required.
whyNot.2: The patient is the first person to be told; waiting for family delays this.
whyNot.3: No permission is required to be open with a patient.

B.q: A patient suffers anxiety after an incident. For it to count as prolonged psychological harm under regulation 20, how long must it last?
options: At least 7 continuous days
At least 14 continuous days
At least 21 continuous days
At least 28 continuous days
B.why: Prolonged psychological harm means psychological harm experienced, or likely to be experienced, for a continuous period of at least 28 days.

whyNot.0: 7 days is shorter than the regulation 20 threshold.
whyNot.1: 14 days is shorter than the regulation 20 threshold.
whyNot.2: 21 days is shorter than the regulation 20 threshold.

C.q: A nurse notices she drew up the wrong insulin, but realises before giving it. No harm occurs. What does the professional duty of candour require of her?
options: Tell the patient and send a formal written apology
Report it locally and judge whether to tell the patient
Note it in the records but make no incident report
Notify the CQC as a notifiable safety incident
C.why: Near misses must be reported in line with the organisation's policy to support learning. Whether to tell the patient is a matter of professional judgement (NMC/GMC guidance paras 21–24).

whyNot.0: Telling the patient about a near miss is a judgement call; a written apology is not routinely required.
whyNot.2: Near misses should be reported through the organisation's system so lessons are learnt, even with no harm.
whyNot.3: A near miss with no harm is not a notifiable safety incident under regulation 20.

C.q: A healthcare assistant tells a staff nurse that the nurse in charge asked her not to report a medication error. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Advise her to follow the nurse in charge's instruction
Report it at the next team meeting without names
Support her to report it and raise the concern
Wait to see if the patient comes to any harm
C.why: Registrants must not try to stop colleagues raising concerns, and must support openness (Code 16.5; NMC/GMC guidance para 28). If someone is discouraged from reporting, a concern should be raised.

whyNot.0: Following an instruction to suppress reporting would support a cover-up.
whyNot.1: A delayed, anonymised mention does not meet the need for prompt reporting.
whyNot.3: The error must be reported now, whether or not harm follows.

C.q: After a pressure ulcer caused by missed repositioning, Mrs Ali, who has capacity, says she does not want to hear the details. What should the nurse do?
options: Respect this, record it and tell her she can ask later
Give the full account anyway to meet the duty
Give the details to her daughter instead
Delay the conversation until she is discharged
C.why: If a patient does not want more information, try to find out why, then respect their wishes as far as possible, record this and make clear they can change their mind at any time (NMC/GMC para 13).

whyNot.1: Forcing information on her ignores her stated wishes.
whyNot.2: Sharing details with her daughter without her agreement breaches confidentiality.
whyNot.3: Delaying is not the issue; she has declined the detail and that must be recorded.

reteach.title: Candour as 'tell, sorry, fix, write'
reteach.question: If you only remember four verbs, can you meet Code 14?

blocks.body: FIX: put the situation right and make the person safe. TELL: explain fully and promptly what happened and the likely effects. SORRY: apologise personally and genuinely. WRITE: document the events and the conversation, report and escalate. The organisation then has its own legal steps under regulation 20 for serious incidents.

blocks.text: Reg 20 is the ORGANISATION's legal duty; Code 14 is YOUR professional duty. You cannot leave candour to the organisation.

explain.body: Every registrant must be open and honest with patients when something that goes wrong causes, or could cause, harm or distress. It is set out in Code 14 and the joint NMC/GMC guidance.

test.q: Which Code standard sets out the professional duty of candour?
options: Standard 10
Standard 16
Standard 20
Standard 14
test.why: Standard 14: be open and candid with all service users about all aspects of care and treatment, including when mistakes or harm have taken place.

whyNot.1: Standard 16 is about acting on risks and raising concerns.
whyNot.2: Standard 20 is about upholding the reputation of the profession.

explain.body: Patients expect to hear what happened, what can be done about any harm, and what will prevent it happening again. A personalised apology ('I am sorry') is more meaningful. Record the apology in the clinical notes.

test.q: According to NMC/GMC guidance, which form of apology do patients usually find most meaningful?
options: A letter from the chief executive
A personal 'I am sorry' from the professional
A general statement of regret from the trust
An apology given by the patient advice service
test.why: Patients are likely to find a personalised apology, such as 'I am sorry', more meaningful than a general expression of regret on the organisation's behalf.

whyNot.0: A formal letter may follow, but a personal apology is more meaningful.
whyNot.2: A general organisational statement is less meaningful than a personal apology.
whyNot.3: The apology should come from the most appropriate team member, not an advice service.

explain.body: Under reg 20, an unintended or unexpected incident that could result in, or appears to have resulted in, death, severe harm, moderate harm or prolonged psychological harm.

test.q: A patient needs an unplanned return to theatre after a retained swab. How is this harm classed under regulation 20?
options: Low harm event
No harm event
Moderate harm
Near miss event
test.why: An unplanned return to surgery is listed as a moderate increase in treatment, which defines moderate harm and makes it a notifiable safety incident.

whyNot.0: Low harm is not a reg 20 notifiable category; a return to theatre exceeds it.
whyNot.1: The patient needed further surgery, so harm occurred.
whyNot.3: A near miss causes no harm; this patient was harmed.

explain.body: As soon as reasonably practicable: notify the relevant person in person, give a true account and an apology, then follow up in writing with results of enquiries and an apology. Keep records.

test.q: Under regulation 20, how must the first notification of a notifiable safety incident be given?
options: In person by a representative of the provider
By letter within 10 working days
By telephone from the ward manager
By email from the patient safety team
test.why: Regulation 20(3)(a): the notification must be given in person by one or more representatives of the registered person, followed by written notification.

whyNot.1: Written notification follows the in-person one; the regulation sets no 10-day letter.
whyNot.2: The regulation requires notification in person, not by telephone.
whyNot.3: Email is not the in-person notification required.
